summary: Summarizes the key features of OSPF version 2 and analyzes how the protocol will perform and scale in the Internet. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is a review of how well a road-map-sharing system for routers will work as things grow.

subtitle: A 1991 report on what OSPF version 2 does and how well it should scale, as required to advance to Draft Standard.

tldr.problem: The IAB and IESG required a report on OSPF's key features, resource use and limits before the routing protocol could advance to Draft Standard status.
tldr.mechanism: The report summarizes OSPF version 2, then estimates link bandwidth, router memory, CPU and Designated Router load, using field statistics from three networks.
tldr.outcome: It concludes that router memory is the most likely limit on OSPF domain size, that OSPF suits transit and small networks, and that it is weak at expressing policy.

facts.label: External LSAs at 56 Kb, 5% of link

today: RFC 1245 is an Informational report from July 1991, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes OSPF version 2 as specified in RFC 1247, and its figures reflect the networks and routers of 1991.

sections.title: Why This Report Exists
sections.content:
RFC 1245 is the first of two reports on OSPF, a TCP/IP routing protocol designed to run inside one Autonomous System, which makes it an Interior Gateway Protocol. The IAB and IESG required these reports before an Internet routing protocol could advance to Draft Standard status.

The report is about OSPF version 2, documented in RFC 1247. Version 1 was published in RFC 1131. The report answers five questions: what the key features are, how much bandwidth, memory and CPU the protocol uses, how that usage scales (at least an order of magnitude beyond the current environment), where the protocol breaks, and which environments suit it.
sections.eli5: Before a new rulebook can become official, grown-ups ask, 'How well does it work, and when does it stop working?' This report is the answer.

sections.title: Key Features of OSPF
sections.content:
OSPF is a link-state (SPF-based) protocol, unlike distance-vector protocols such as RIP. Small link state advertisements (LSAs) each describe one piece of the domain: a router's neighborhood, a transit network's neighborhood, one inter-area route or one external route. They are flooded reliably, so every router holds an identical link state database. Each router then runs the Dijkstra procedure to build a shortest-path tree rooted at itself.

The report lists many further features:

  • Designated Router and Backup Designated Router on multi-access networks, so the backup can take over without redoing adjacency bring-up.
  • Areas, which protect routing inside an area from outside information and reduce Dijkstra cost.
  • Separate LSAs for each external route, a forwarding address, type 1 and type 2 external metrics, and a 32-bit external route tag.
  • A four level hierarchy: intra-area, inter-area, external type 1 and external type 2 routes.
  • Virtual links, authentication of every routing packet, equal-cost multipath, TOS-based routing, variable-length subnet masks and stub areas.
sections.eli5: Every router draws the same map of the roads and then works out its own best routes from it. Areas are like splitting a huge map into neighborhood maps so each one is easier to handle.

sections.title: Field Data, Bandwidth, Memory and CPU
sections.content:
The report draws on statistics from three deployed networks (BARRNet, NSI and OARnet). LSAs are refreshed at least every 30 minutes, and measured database turnover was close to that on all three. About three LSAs travel in each packet, and flooding retransmits were 1.3%, 1.4% and 0.7%, so they can be ignored in the bandwidth estimate. Dijkstra ran only every 13 to 50 minutes on average.

Bandwidth. Taking an AS external LSA of 36 bytes plus one third of a packet header gives 52 bytes sent every 30 minutes, an average of 23/100 bits per second. Limiting routing traffic to 5% of a link allows 2087 external advertisements on a 9.6 Kb line and 12,174 on a 56 Kb line. The report says OSPF uses considerably less bandwidth than RIP.

Memory. The report estimates 64 bytes per external LSA once support data is included, so 10,000 external LSAs use 640K bytes. OSPF definitely needs more memory than RIP.

CPU. In a sparse network with a bounded number of interfaces per router, Dijkstra is of order n * log(n). A figure cited from Steve Deering's work gives around 15 milliseconds for 200 routers. Because Dijkstra runs so rarely, the report expects OSPF to use less CPU than RIP overall, and areas can limit the cost further.
sections.eli5: Sharing the map costs very little talking, because each piece is only re-sent about every half hour. The main thing a router needs is enough room to remember the whole map.

sections.title: Designated Router Load and Limits
sections.content:
Every router on a network multicasts Hello packets, generally every 10 seconds. The Designated Router sends more Link State Updates and receives acknowledgments from all attached routers, so any traffic limit would show up there first. The report does not expect that limit to be reached: more than 50 routers were simulated on one LAN, and 13 routers were attached to one ethernet in interoperability testing without problems.

The harder case is when both the Designated Router and the Backup fail together. The new DR must then synchronize with every other router, which may matter when many routers share one network. A LAN with too many routers can be split into pieces.

The summary names router memory as the most likely limit. A figure of 10,000 external LSAs fits one configuration of the Proteon P4200, while the largest field network, BARRNet, had 1816. Ways to shrink the database include default routing, an EGP that carries its own information, stub areas, and a less flat address space.
sections.eli5: If too many kids crowd into one classroom, the class monitor gets the busiest. You can fix that by splitting the class into smaller rooms.

sections.title: Suitable and Unsuitable Environments
sections.content:
The report says OSPF suits environments from large to small. It is particularly suited to transit Autonomous Systems, because it can hold many external routes, import them flexibly, and update them partially when one changes. It also suits smaller stand-alone or stub Autonomous Systems thanks to fast convergence, equal-cost multipath, TOS routing and areas.

Its weakness is policy. OSPF has very limited ability to express policy, and its only mechanism is the four level routing hierarchy. A system needing richer policy would have to be split into separate Autonomous Systems running a policy-based EGP between them. The memo has no security discussion: it states that security issues are not discussed.
sections.eli5: OSPF works well for both big and small networks, but it is not good at 'only let this traffic through that door' style rules.
